newsitem.title: UK: Yen risk reversal seen catching central banks' eye.
newsitem.headline: Yen risk reversal seen catching central banks' eye.

text.p: Dollar/yen's plunge has led to an extreme bias for yen calls in currency options and this is seen attracting the attention of central banks, reawakening the prospect of near-term intervention to steady markets, options dealers said.

The demand for yen calls was apparent in the dollar/yen risk reversal, an indicator of the market's directional bias which is the difference in implied volatility between equally out-of-the-money calls against relative puts.
The risk reversal was pushed up to a mid-price level of 2.5 percent favouring yen calls in morning Europe on Wednesday as the dollar/yen spot rate plumbed its lowest levels in almost seven months.
The one-month risk reversal has jumped from 1.7 percent seen at the beginning of this week after holding just above 1.0 percent all last week.

"The one-month risk reversal is now being paid above two percent which is usually a good indicator that central bank intervention is due," said Ian Groome, forex options trader at ABN Amro Bank in London.

The U.S. Federal Reserve is a noted watcher of currency option risk reversals to ascertain the market's directional bias. The one-month dollar/yen risk reversal was last at current levels in August 1995 when central banks intervened to prop the dollar when it was trading just above 85 yen.
At the time of the Fed's intervention in August 1995, the dollar/yen risk reversal was skewed in favour of dollar calls, a factor which dealers said made the concerted intervention so successful.

In April 1995 when dollar/yen stood at record lows just below 80 yen, the risk reversal had an extreme skew to yen calls -- again, above 2.0 percent. Although the Bank of Japan was intervening by buying dollars at this time, it was going against the grain of the market and the shift in sentiment towards dollar upside was more gradual.

"People do perceive this (2.0 percent risk reversal) level as a potential central bank buying level, at least it's got their attention," said a UK bank options dealer. "But historically, the risk reversal seems to be at its top and, on its own, is not likely to spur central bank action for the moment."
Although a valuable tool for central banks, dealers the risk reversal was only one indicator among many for gauging their intervention strategy.
Also, most of the recent options activity has been in the short-end of the market and purely reactive of moves in the spot rate, with little directional plays emerging.

"It is too early to speak of a fundamental shift in sentiment," said Satu Jaatinen, vp on Chase Manhattan Investment Bank's options desk. "If the one-year options get as excited as the short-dates, then that would be interesting."

One-month dollar/yen volatility stood at 14.6/15.0 percent at midday Europe, slightly off earlier highs but well above late Tuesday's 13.6/14.1 percent. One-year vols traded at 11.5/11.7 percent against 10.9/11.2.

The fall in the dollar/yen spot rate, which tested a fresh low of 110.62 earlier on Wednesday, has been attributed mainly to concern the U.S. will take issue with Japan's widening trade surplus with Washington.

"We see too much emphasis being put on the U.S.-Japan trade issue and dollar/yen vols look overdone on that basis," said one trader. "A break of 110 probably will see vols knee-jerk higher but the extreme bias of the risk reversal won't last and should limit big vol gains from here."
